did_you_know.text: The word katit is related to a verb meaning “to crush” or “to pound.” It refers to olive oil made from crushed olives and intended to burn cleanly in the lamp.
The twelve loaves are commonly understood as recalling the twelve tribes of Israel. They were baked as large loaves and arranged before God.
Frankincense is an aromatic resin collected from trees and was used in both worship and perfumes in the ancient world. Its rising fragrance symbolized the offering being lifted up.
The Hebrew phrase lechem ha-panim literally means “bread of the Presence” or “bread of the faces.” In English it is often called showbread, because it was set before God.

This is one of the Bible’s few stories about a person whose father was Egyptian and whose mother was Israelite. The story first describes a quarrel in the camp, without presenting his ancestry itself as a crime.

The verb va-yikkov is basically related to piercing or making a hole, but here it describes a hostile utterance against God’s name. In Jewish tradition, the name YHWH is generally not pronounced as it is written.

The phrase “eye for eye” sets a principle of proportional response, not permission for unlimited revenge. The Sages interpreted it as requiring financial compensation rather than causing an identical bodily injury.

Here the word ger refers to a foreign resident living among the Israelites, not necessarily someone who underwent conversion in the later sense. The verse emphasizes that the resident foreigner and the citizen should be subject to the same law.
